result.why:
I could not refute this from the code. The main claim holds, and the impact is smaller than the finding suggests.

What the code does (C:\ct\test-sites\tambola\apps\web\public\z.js):
- Line 771 sets `awake = v.phase === "play" && ... && !v.locked && !v.paused && !v.stopped && (v.log.length > 0 || ...)` and calls `keepAwake(awake)`. When `v.paused` becomes true, `keepAwake(false)` releases the wake lock at lines 759-761.
- The comment on that line says the lock is held "to the end of the game", and the one-line comment at 757 says its purpose is to stop a locked phone missing numbers. A pause sits inside that range, so the code contradicts its own comment.
- The release is inconsistent with the other states. Scheduled breaks (`v.brk`), intermission and host-called "hold" mode all keep the lock, and hold can wait much longer than a pause. An organizer pause is the one state with no end time on the page: the banner at line 662 says only "Paused by the organizer. It will carry on shortly."
- A pause can last up to `maxPauseRounds`, which is 600 rounds, about 30 minutes (config in `control.ts`, defaults at lines 386 and 390). That is far longer than any phone's screen timeout.
- The release also restarts the phone's idle timer, so the phone locks soon after the pause starts.
- When the organizer resumes, the locked page is hidden and cannot call `keepAwake`. The `visibilitychange` handler at line 767 only re-acquires the lock after the person unlocks the phone, which they have no reason to do at that moment.

Why a missed number is lost:
- `callCard` (about lines 614-625) shows only the latest number.
- The ticket never marks itself (line 658: "the ticket never marks itself").
- I found no history strip, no "you were away" message and no catch-up message (grep for "were away" returned nothing).
- The claim window is `CLAIM_WINDOW_CALLS = 1`: a claim must arrive before the next number is called.
- So numbers called after a resume while the phone is locked cannot be recovered from the screen.

Why it is only low:
- No number is called during a pause, and a claim made during the pause still counts. The damage starts only if the phone is locked at the moment of resume and stays locked for a few calls.
- This is a gap in a new, best-effort feature. Version 1.1.8 had no wake lock at all, so it is not a regression.
- The pause release was deliberate. The originally confirmed audit fix (`idiotproof-confirmed.json`, the player-pages wake-lock item) also contained `!v.paused`, but the reason is weak.
- Holding the screen for up to 30 minutes costs a little battery.
- No test expects the lock to be released on pause. The only wake-lock test (`apps/web/test/idiotproof-player-pages.test.ts`, "the screen is held awake only from about a minute before the first number...") checks the start of the game, not a pause.

result.title: Check-in: the red 'Before you press Submit: tick ...' message is not cleared when the person ticks the boxes, so it keeps telling them to do what they have just done
result.scenario: The person types the 4-digit code and presses Submit before ticking. The new check sets CK.err = 'Before you press Submit: tick "This name is correct", tick "This mobile number is correct".' and shows it in #ckerr. They tick both boxes. The change handler in chk() only sets x[key] and calls sync(), which hides the hint line but does not touch CK.err or #ckerr, and the 1 s redraw rebuilds the same error text. The screen now shows both boxes ticked, the hint hidden, and a red alert still saying to tick them. Only typing in a box (hook()) clears it.
result.fix: In chk() in C:\ct\test-sites\tambola\apps\web\public\z.js (line 740), clear the message the same way hook() does: `el.onchange = () => { x[key] = el.checked; CK.err = ""; const e = $("ckerr"); if (e) e.textContent = ""; sync(); };`. Optionally add a test step in idiotproof-player-pages.test.ts that ticks both boxes after the early Submit press and expects `#ckerr` to be empty.
result.why:
The defect is real in z.js at commit 274bde8. The new submit check at line 745 sets `CK.err = "Before you press Submit: " + miss.join(", ") + "."` and writes it to `#ckerr` (a role=alert element). The only places that clear `CK.err` are the `hook()` oninput handler (line 737) and the start of a real submit (line 746) or a success (line 751). The checkbox handler `chk()` (line 740) is `el.onchange = () => { x[key] = el.checked; sync(); }`. `sync()` only saves to storage and toggles the `#ckhint` line, so it never touches `CK.err` or `#ckerr`.

`checkinView()` renders `${CK.err ? esc(CK.err) : ""}` into `#ckerr` on every redraw, so the 1 s `paint()` loop rebuilds the same text. If a checkbox still has focus, `paint()` skips the redraw (the `/^ck/` focus guard). Once focus moves, the redraw shows both boxes checked, the hint hidden, and the red alert still saying to tick them. The Edit buttons force a redraw that also keeps the message. A typed digit does clear it, but a person whose code was already typed will not type again. The stale text goes away only when they press Submit, which clears it at line 746.

The new check is what introduced this. In fdf52e7 `CK.err` was set only after a server response, so this stale state did not exist there. The existing test (`idiotproof-player-pages.test.ts` line 105) only checks that the message appears after an early press, not that it clears after the boxes are ticked, so no test covers this.

Impact is small. Submit stays enabled, so pressing it still works and the person is not blocked or losing data. Still, the screen contradicts itself and breaks the owner rule that error messages say what to do and sit beside the control used. The suggested fix is correct and matches how `hook()` already behaves. It also clears a stale server message such as a wrong code once the person changes a box, which is harmless.

result.title: Organizer console tries the relay last, with no timeout, so Next number / Pause hang on a network that drops drand traffic
result.scenario: beaconRound() loops `[...MIRRORS, ...relay()]` one at a time with a bare fetch() (no AbortSignal). On an office network that silently drops traffic to the drand servers (the 'stalls at 0 of 90' case the release describes), each of the 4 direct fetches hangs until the browser's own connect timeout, and the relay is only reached after all four. TBControl.sign() awaits this before every message. In a Host-mode game the 'Next number' button (zc.js nextnum handler, no timeout) stays on 'pressing' and no number can be released. The Pause/Resume/Stop buttons give up after their 30 s race with a connection error. The same-origin relay is the one route guaranteed to work (the console page itself loaded from this site), yet it is the last one tried.
result.fix:
In packages/beacon/src/control-browser.ts, change beaconRound() in three ways. Then rebuild control.js (`bun run build:control`).
1. Put the relay first: `[...relay(), ...MIRRORS]`. It is the one route that works wherever the console page loaded.
2. Give every fetch a short abort, about 3-4 s. Use an AbortController plus setTimeout rather than AbortSignal.timeout, because the file already supports older Safari and Firefox. The abort must also cover `r.json()`.
3. Better still, ask the relay and the mirrors in parallel and take the first valid answer (Promise.any-style, with a shared 4-5 s overall cap). The clock-computed round is the last resort only, since nextMessage documents that the round should come from the beacon, not a skewed device clock.

Optionally remember a mirror that failed or timed out in a module-level variable, so later presses skip it, as the phone runtime's `downUntil` does.

Separately, make the zc.js nextnum handler time out like the 30 s race on the Pause/Resume/Stop buttons, so S.pressing cannot stay set indefinitely.
result.why:
The code does what the finding describes. In control-browser.ts, beaconRound() (lines 29-34) awaits `[...MIRRORS, ...relay()]` one at a time. Each call is a bare `fetch()` with no AbortSignal. The same-origin relay is last. TBControl.sign() (line 62) awaits this before every signed message, and publish() calls sign(). Nothing else bounds it:
- CSP connect-src in pages/build.mjs allows the four drand hosts, so the direct fetches really go out.
- blackbox.js and rum.js wrap window.fetch but add no timeout.
- The control.js bundle contains the same code, so the relay edit did ship.
- control-browser.ts says it is not unit-tested, and the console tests replace TBControl.sign with a stub. No test covers this path.

Nothing makes the 'Next number' handler (zc.js:1898-1907) give up. It sets S.pressing = true and awaits TBControl.publish(...) with no timeout, and a second press is ignored while pressing is true. The Pause, Resume and Stop buttons (zc.js:1911) race publish against a 30 s timer and show a connection error. The underlying publish keeps running in the background and can still land later.

I would not call it high, for these reasons:
1. It is not a regression. Before the release the same four un-timed fetches ran, then the code fell back to the device clock. The release only added the relay as a fifth, last source. The nextnum and ctl handlers are not in the diff.
2. It only bites a network that silently drops traffic to the drand hosts. A firewall that resets the connection, serves a block page, has DNS blocking, or has a proxy answering 403 fails fast, because `r.ok` is false or fetch throws, and then falls through to the relay quickly.
3. It is a delay, not a permanent block. After the four fetches give up, the relay is reached and the press succeeds. The finding's 'no number can be released' is overstated. The delay is at least the browser connect timeout, which I put at roughly 20-30 s per host on desktop Chrome, so about 1.5-2 minutes or more per press.
4. It affects Host-mode 'Next number' presses, Pause/Resume/Stop, and the confirm.js sign path.

It is still a real gap against the release's own claim. The 1.2.0 notes say a company firewall 'no longer stalls a game at 0 of 90 numbers'. The phone runtime handles this properly: parallel hedged requests, a 6 s timeout, and `downUntil` memory so blocked hosts are asked last. The organizer's signing helper does none of this and keeps no memory between presses, so every press repeats the full wait. A Host-mode organizer on the same blocked office network still has a game that effectively stalls. During a live game with real participants that is a stuck-organizer case.

result.title: fetchBackfill ignores the new 'blocked mirror asked last' logic, so catching up on a blocked network costs ~24 s per batch
result.scenario: fetchBackfill() walks the mirror list in fixed order, one single-mirror fetchRound() at a time, until two mirrors agree. It never consults isDown() (index.ts) and the relay is the last entry. On a network that drops packets to the drand servers, each of the 4 direct probes waits the full default 6 s timeout, so 24 s pass before the relay is asked. The relay is only one answer (answers.length < 2), so the code then falls back to fetchLive(). phone-runtime.tick uses fetchBackfill for every round more than 2 behind and awaits all 8 in one Promise.all. A phone that was locked or backgrounded for a minute, or that joined late, therefore gets numbers in batches of 8 about 25 s apart, about as slow as the game itself. It stays far enough behind to miss claim windows. The 'asked last' fix only reaches fetchLive.
result.fix:
Smallest change, in packages/beacon/src/index.ts and game.ts. Export `isDown` from index.ts, import it in game.ts, and in the `fetchBackfill` loop skip any mirror that is currently marked down. Check it on every iteration, not once up front, so marks set by concurrent rounds in the same batch count:

  const m = mirrors[(i + salt) % mirrors.length]!;
  if (isDown(m)) continue;

The existing `answers.length < 2` fallback then goes straight to `fetchLive`, which already asks the relay first. The first batch then costs about 6 s instead of 24 s, and later batches cost almost nothing. For the stall to stay short:
- Make the 'down' memory outlast a catch-up burst. Raise DOWN_FOR, or count it per tick instead of per request. At 8 or more requests per second, 40 requests is only a few seconds.
- Optionally add a re-entrancy guard around `rt.tick()` in the z.js `loop()`, so a slow tick does not stack up duplicate backfills.
- Optionally do not mark a mirror down when it was only aborted by `finish()` after another mirror won (index.ts, the `.catch` at line ~105).
result.why:
The mechanism is real, but it is narrower than reported and is not a regression, so I rate it low instead of medium.

What the code does (274bde8):
- `fetchBackfill` (game.ts ~291-306) loops over `this.opts.mirrors ?? defaultMirrors()`. Production pages use `new ZG.RoundStore({})` and `beacon: {}` (z.js:69, big.js:12, zc.js:1423), so the list is the 4 drand hosts plus the relay, and the relay is last.
- Each iteration awaits a single-mirror `fetchRound(..., { mirrors: [one] })`. Reordering by `isDown` cannot do anything to a one-element list, and `isDown` is never read in game.ts. It is a non-exported const in index.ts.
- The default timeout is 6000 ms (index.ts:94), and nothing in production overrides it.
- If all 4 direct hosts silently drop packets, the loop spends 4 x 6 s = 24 s. The relay then gives only 1 answer, so `answers.length < 2` sends it to `fetchLive`, which does put the relay first. One batch therefore costs about 24 s plus a small amount.
- `tick()` (phone-runtime.ts:384) uses `fetchBackfill` for any round more than 2 behind. That covers a late joiner or a phone resuming after being locked. The 8 rounds in a batch run in one `Promise.all`.
- The finding's claim that the 'asked last' fix only reaches `fetchLive` is correct.

Why it is not worse:
- It only bites when the direct hosts hang. A fast failure (DNS block, reset, proxy block page) fails instantly. The relay-client test models the firewall as an immediate throw, and that case is fast.
- It is not a regression. The live version (fdf52e7) used a hardcoded list of the 4 direct hosts only, with no relay. On such a network backfill spent the same 24 s and then failed. Release 1.2.0 turns 'never works' into 'works slowly'. Live play (`now - br <= 2`) goes through `fetchLive` and is not affected.
- Catch-up still converges. Batches of 8 per ~25 s are faster than the game's one call per 6 s or longer.

What makes it worse than the finding says:
- z.js:843-844 runs `setInterval(loop, 1000)` with no re-entrancy guard (phone-runtime.ts:105 even admits ticks overlap).
- During a 25 s backfill, about 25 more ticks start. Each rebuilds the same `want` set, because the store is still empty, and launches its own sequential 5-probe chains, so one phone sends many duplicate requests.
- `askCount` rises by about 8 per second during catch-up. That also shortens the 40-request 'down' memory to a few seconds, so the 'asked last' benefit is partly lost.

The stalled tick delays `autoClaim`, but only for a phone that is already behind.

I did not run anything, per the brief. The timing is derived from the code.

result.title: TBControl.sign() builds its sequence number from the 1-second shared copy of the pause file
result.scenario: sharedRead() serves any GET of /api/z/<id>/control without an x-organizer or Authorization header from the Cache API for up to 1 s, and a publish does not purge it. sign() reads the file anonymously (`fetch(url, {cache:"no-store"})`, no auth header) and nextMessage() sets `seq = f.messages.length + 1`. In a live game phones keep the cache warm. A Host presses Next number and, within the same second, presses Pause or Stop. The second message is built from the old copy, reuses the same seq, and the server answers 409 'That sequence number is already used.', which the console shows raw. (The same stale copy is used by ensureKey at line 44 and the console's own read at zc.js:1412, but those self-heal on the next refresh.)
result.fix:
Best root-cause fix: purge the shared copy on a successful write. In apps/edge/src/worker.ts, after `publishControl` succeeds in the POST handler (about line 1280), and after `registerKey` and `addHostKey` succeed, call `await (globalThis as any).caches?.default?.delete(new Request(req.url, { method: "GET" }))` inside a try/catch. This is the same key sharedRead uses. It fixes the console's own read (zc.js:1413), ensureKey and sign(), while other data centres stay within the designed 1 s.

Smallest client-only alternative: in control-browser.ts sign(), send `headers: hdr(a)` on the GET so it bypasses the share. The POST already sends that header with an empty token from confirm.js, so it is harmless. The cost is one extra audited request per press.

Also change the `ctlWords` text for "already used" to say plainly that this press did not go through and should be pressed again in a few seconds.
result.why:
The defect is real, was introduced by 1.2.0, and has a narrow window with little impact.

What the code shows:
- **sharedRead is new in 1.2.0.** At fdf52e7 the control GET at worker.ts:1207 had no cache wrapper. At 274bde8 it is wrapped at worker.ts:1261 in `sharedRead(req, 1, ...)`.
- **The share keys on URL only and skips only authed calls.** sharedRead (worker.ts:234-243) bypasses the cache only if `x-organizer` or `authorization` is present. Otherwise it serves `cache.match(new Request(req.url))` for up to 1 s.
- **No purge on publish.** A grep of worker.ts finds `caches` only at lines 219, 235 and 1261. The POST handler (worker.ts:1273-1281) never calls `cache.delete`.
- **sign() reads anonymously.** control-browser.ts:59 does `fetch(url, {cache:"no-store"})` with no auth header. `cache:"no-store"` only controls the browser's own cache and does not stop the Worker's share. So sign() can get a copy up to 1 s old.
- **A stale copy gives a reused seq.** `nextMessage` (control.ts:433) uses `seq = f.messages.length + 1`. `publishControl` (control.ts:407) then answers 409 "That sequence number is already used." because the sig differs.
- **The cache is warm in a live game.** CONTROL_R2 is commented out in wrangler.toml, so phones poll `/api/z/<id>/control` through the Worker (phone-runtime.ts:320). The console (zc.js:1413) and the big screen (big.js:20) read the same URL anonymously.
- **No test covers it.** Worker tests run without `caches`, and control-browser.ts is not unit tested.

Why it is only low:
- **The window is under 1 s.** The host must send a second signed action within that time of the first action being accepted. For a human that is about 0.3 s on average.
- **It self-heals.** The 409 loses nothing and a second press a moment later works. Double-taps are already blocked by `S.pressing` and `S.ctlBusy`.

Corrections to the report:
- **The text is not always raw.** The Pause, Resume, Stop and Extend path (zc.js:1911) maps the 409 through `ctlWords` (zc.js:999) to "A press went through just before this one. Look at the buttons to see where the game is now." Only the Next path (zc.js:1904) shows the server text raw.
- **That mapped message misleads.** If the host's second press was an emergency Pause, it does not say the Pause failed or tell them to press again.
- **The ensureKey point is trivial.** A stale `pub` read at control-browser.ts:44 does not matter in practice.
- **Host-key lag is unreachable in practice.** The same stale copy could briefly hide a Host key just added, since sign() checks `f.hostKeys` at line 61. Nobody presses a control within 1 s of page load.

result.title: Held demo-pass secrets (loginpass/<emailhash>) are never swept and stay usable
result.scenario: holdPassForSignIn() stores the raw one-time pass secret `{t: tok, at}` in kv under `loginpass/<email hash>`. The key is only removed by useHeldPass() on a successful organizer sign-in. If the person never finishes signing in, or the address belongs to a Host-only account (acct is null so useHeldPass is never called), the row stays forever. retentionSweep() lists start/, linkfail/, plim/, jlim/, jbm/, penr/, delreq/, seen/ and alert/ but not loginpass/. The 2-hour expiry is checked only when the row is read. A plain-text copy of an unredeemed pass link therefore sits in the database indefinitely, although the design keeps only hashes of these secrets in code.
result.fix:
1. In retentionSweep (apps/edge/src/worker.ts, near line 2058), add a separate `safe(...)` step. It should SELECT k, v FROM kv WHERE k LIKE 'loginpass/%' LIMIT 2000, parse each v, and DELETE the row when `now - Number(JSON.parse(v).at) > 2 * 3_600_000`, or when the value is unreadable. Do not reuse the penr/delreq loop: that loop reads `.t`, which here is the secret string, so the comparison would be NaN and never match.
2. Optionally, call `await env.DB.prepare("DELETE FROM kv WHERE k=?").bind(`loginpass/${row.email_hash}`)` on the Host-only path. Or skip holding the pass when `acct` is null, since only organizer accounts can redeem it.
3. Add a `loginpass/` row to the docs/RETENTION.md table (2 hours, deleted by the sweep), and a case to apps/edge/test/retention.test.ts that seeds an old and a fresh loginpass row.
4. Stronger alternative: store only the pass hash (`ph`) in the kv row and change redeemDemoPass/useHeldPass to take the hash. That way no raw secret is ever written to the database.
result.why:
The finding holds up in the code, and nothing else handles it. The scope is narrow: it is a retention and secret-hygiene gap, and no person is blocked or confused.

What I checked:
- holdPassForSignIn (apps/edge/src/worker.ts:352-356) writes the raw 32-hex pass secret into kv as `loginpass/<emailhash>`, with value `{t: tok, at: now}`. It is stored in plain text, not as the `ph` hash the code otherwise keeps.
- The only delete is in useHeldPass (line 361). Every caller is guarded by `if (acct)` (lines 984, 1003, 1017).
- Two cases leave the row behind:
  - The person asks for a code and never finishes signing in.
  - The address belongs to a Host-only account (`hostAcct` set, `acct` null). Both /api/start (line 887) and /api/auth/email (line 903) still call holdPassForSignIn for it. useHeldPass is never reached, because redeemDemoPass needs an organizer org. That row can never be consumed.
- The 2-hour expiry (`now - x.at <= 2 * 3_600_000`, line 362) is checked only when the row is read, so it never removes anything on its own.
- retentionSweep (lines 2048-2066) covers start/, linkfail/, plim/, jlim/, jbm/, penr/, delreq/, seen/ and alert/. It does not cover `loginpass/`.
- `loginpass` does not appear in docs/RETENTION.md, so this record also breaks the retention schedule the product publishes.
- apps/edge/test/retention.test.ts has no loginpass case. The only test expectations (demo-pass.test.ts:65 and 74) cover the happy path and the made-up-secret case.
- It is new in 1.2.0: `git log -S loginpass` shows it first appears in commit dcf563a, which is part of the fdf52e7..274bde8 range.

Why the severity is low:
- The held secrets are demo-pass links, each worth one free 100- or 250-person game, valid until 31 Dec 2026 and single use.
- Exploiting this needs read access to the D1 database or its backups.
- The design comment (lines ~302-306) promises "only hashes of the links" are kept, and that promise is about the repository, not the database.
- Beyond the plain-text secret, the leftover key is also an email-hash-keyed record kept without a limit.

One flaw in the suggested fix: the existing `penr/` and `delreq/` sweep reads `JSON.parse(v).t` as a timestamp. In loginpass rows `t` is the token string. `now - "<hex>"` is NaN, so `NaN > DAY` is false and nothing would ever be deleted. loginpass therefore needs its own branch that reads `at`.

The home screen (no game open) opens the 'Your account' box by default (S.acctOpen = null, zc.js:1346, so open = !eid). Its keys list prints k.kind === "ai" ? result.fix:
In apps/web/public/zc.js acctHtml(), around lines 1179-1180:

result.why:
The finding holds. I read all of it in the release tree at 274bde8.

1. Every organizer has an AI key. createOrganizer (apps/edge/src/worker.ts:649) inserts an organizer_key row with kind "ai" at sign-up. GET /api/org/keys (worker.ts:1051-1056) selects every key row for the org, whether active or revoked, and returns each row's kind unchanged.

   - aiBlock() returns "" (zc.js:1167).

5. Nothing else catches it. pages.test.ts:221 checks p.text() only on a game screen (UI-TEN), where the account box is collapsed, and it only tests /AI work link/. No test asserts "AI assistant link", "Organizer key" or the retire button text on the home screen. Lines 1188 and 1201 (actBanner, "Your AI assistant is asking") are reached only after an AI hand-over, so they are not the main problem.
